title: Hi, I’m Roberta Colapietro!
text: A PhD student in chronobiology, I study how our body’s internal clock works and how it gets broken in disease. As a medical doctor, I hope to one day turn these findings into real improvements for patients. In the meantime, as a science communicator, I strive to make the science of our internal clock accessible to everyone, with a dash of color and a pinch of fun.

title: Science Communication
text: I strongly believe that doing good science is just as important as sharing it with the public. As a science communicator, I experiment with different formats to share scientific knowledge.

title: Science Communication
text:
Workshops for kids
This is the format I started with as a student at the University of Pavia, demonstrating experiments about the human body at Indiscienza, a student-organized science fair. Later, I came back to this format by organizing workshops for Italian children in Germany with the association Native Scientist, and workshops in German for local children as part of the KinderUni at the University of Cologne.

title: Science Communication
text:
Video
This was a one-off, but a lot of fun! Together with other science communication enthusiasts from the association Indiscienza, I made a stop-motion video (in Italian) about antibiotic resistance, which won the Italian National Prize for Science Outreach in the category “Short videos”.

title: About me
text:
© Tanio Calabrese



I am a PhD student at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, where I study how the clocks inside our cells relate to human health.
In the Buchauer Lab, I develop computational methods to infer the internal time of individual cells. By combining biological insight with computational approaches, I aim to understand how cells fall out of sync and what role this desynchronization may play in disease.
My path into research began during medical school at the University of Pavia, Italy, where I complemented my clinical training with international research experiences in mitochondria, metabolism and, finally, chronobiology. After graduating as a medical doctor, I chose to dedicate myself fully to research, which led me to pursue a PhD. Medicine, however, taught me to ask biological questions with an eye on what they mean for patients, so bringing my findings from bench to bedside remains a goal close to my heart.
Beyond the lab, I am a passionate science communicator. I love sharing the wonders of science with different formats of scientific outreach.
